hints: Think of the three domains in the classification system and pick out which ones are made up of prokaryotic cells with no membrane-bound nucleus.
walkthrough:
Remember What Prokaryotic Means**
Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. In the three-domain system there are only two prokaryotic domains, and the third domain Eukarya contains all eukaryotes.

Name Both Prokaryotic Domains**
The two prokaryotic domains are Bacteria and Archaea, so both are natural sources of restriction endonucleases.

hints: Start by thinking how you would get hold of just the coding sequence for that one enzyme in large enough amounts to work with.
Think about the usual carrier DNA used to carry a foreign gene into E. coli and what enzymes are needed to open it and join the new gene in.
Think how the carrier DNA is actually put into E. coli cells and why only some cells will take it up.
Think how you would find the successful transformed cells and then grow them up to make a lot of enzyme economically.
walkthrough:
Get and Copy the Gene**
Isolate the gene coding for the specific restriction endonuclease from the donor bacterial DNA, or synthesise it from nucleotides / from mRNA. Then use PCR to make many copies of the gene so there is enough DNA to work with.

Build a Recombinant Plasmid**
Cut open a plasmid vector with a restriction enzyme to create sticky ends. Mix the gene with the cut plasmid so complementary sticky ends anneal, then join them with DNA ligase which forms phosphodiester bonds. This gives a recombinant plasmid carrying the gene plus a promoter for continuous expression.

Put the Plasmid into E. coli**
Transform E. coli by adding the recombinant plasmids to the cells and treating with calcium ions and heat shock, or electroporation, to make the membranes permeable so plasmids enter.

Select, Grow and Harvest**
Use plasmid marker genes, such as antibiotic resistance, to select and identify only the bacteria with recombinant plasmids. Culture these bacteria in large volume / in a fermenter so they express the gene continuously, then extract and purify the restriction endonuclease.

Final answer: Obtain the restriction endonuclease gene from donor DNA and amplify by PCR; cut plasmid vector with restriction enzyme to give sticky ends; join gene into plasmid with DNA ligase to form recombinant plasmid; transform into E. coli e.g. using heat shock / Ca2+ ions / electroporation; select using marker genes then culture in fermenter and extract / purify enzyme.

hints: Think about the size of the problem - over 3500 enzymes each with a DNA and amino acid sequence - and why a computer store is needed.
Think about what scientists in different labs gain by being able to access the same central store very quickly.
Think about practical uses once sequences are stored together, such as comparing them or working out what the enzyme looks like and which one to choose.
walkthrough:
Handle Huge Amounts of Data**
Databases can store the very large amount of nucleotide, base and amino acid sequence data for thousands of restriction endonucleases in one organised place.

Share and Compare Quickly**
Data can be shared worldwide and accessed quickly. Researchers can compare sequences to look for similarities, evolutionary relationships and conserved recognition sites.

Use Data to Choose and Design**
Stored sequences can be used to predict, model and visualise the 3D structure of the enzyme. This helps identify which restriction endonuclease to use for a particular sequence and helps discover new restriction endonucleases.

Final answer: Store large amounts of nucleotide / base / amino acid sequence data; allow rapid sharing and access; allow comparison of sequences; allow prediction / modelling / visualisation of enzyme structure; allow identification of best enzyme to use or discovery of new enzymes.

hints: Start with the big similarity - think what both methods are actually for when you have a mixture.
Think what type of mixture each method is famous for in this syllabus - DNA or protein versus leaf pigments or amino acids - and what support each mixture moves through.
Think what makes the substances move and separate in each case - electricity versus liquid solvent - and which property matters most.
Think how you see the results and how you identify each spot or band, such as DNA ladder versus $R_f$ value.
walkthrough:
State the Common Role**
Both are separation techniques. A mixture is applied and its components move at different rates so they become separated into bands or spots. Both can separate molecules partly by mass / size.

Compare What Is Separated and On What**
Electrophoresis typically separates DNA, RNA or proteins supported in a gel such as agarose or polyacrylamide. Paper chromatography typically separates photosynthetic pigments or amino acids supported on paper, glass or silica gel.

Compare How Separation Happens**
In electrophoresis movement is driven by an electric current / electric field, and separation depends on charge / polarity and length / mass, with negatively charged DNA moving to the positive electrode. In chromatography movement is driven by a solvent / mobile phase, and separation depends mainly on solubility in the solvent and adsorption to the stationary phase.

Compare Visualisation and Identification**
In electrophoresis bands are visualised with dyes, ethidium bromide and UV light and identified by comparison to a DNA ladder of known lengths or using a DNA probe. In chromatography pigments are seen directly as different colours without added dye or UV, and spots are identified by calculating $R_f$ value and comparing to known reference values.

Final answer: Similarity: both are separation techniques involving movement of substances, e.g. both can separate by mass. Differences: electrophoresis separates DNA / RNA / proteins through gel by electric current / electric field according to charge / polarity / length / mass, visualised with dyes / ethidium bromide / UV light and identified with DNA ladder / DNA probe; chromatography separates pigments / amino acids on paper / silica by solvent according to solubility / mass, visualised as coloured spots and identified by $R_f$ value.
